gloss_terse: beat, knock, drive hard (animals or persons)
gloss_readable: This verb describes forceful, repetitive striking. It appears when Jacob fears his flocks will be 'driven hard' (Gen 33:13), when wicked men 'beat against the door' demanding violent satisfaction (Judg 19:22), and in the lover's cry 'Listen! my beloved is knocking' (Song 5:2). The multilingual evidence captures both senses: the violent driving or pushing (Spanish empujasen, French overdrive) and the percussive knocking (Spanish golpeando, German beating).

senses.1: The three contexts show physical beating or knocking: driving animals cruelly (Gen 33:13), pounding violently on a door (Judg 19:22 'beat themselves tired'), and knocking for entry (Song 5:2). The cross-lingual glosses consistently reflect this dual semantic range of forceful impact, whether applied to livestock or doors.

gloss_terse: fat, rich, vigorous; full of sap or oil
gloss_readable: This adjective evokes abundance and vitality. It describes bread as 'rich' from fertile soil (Isa 30:23), the righteous as trees 'full of sap' and flourishing (Ps 92:14), and 'the prosperous of earth' who bow before God (Ps 22:29). The Spanish rico and French gras ('fatty, rich') highlight the sense of prosperity and well-nourished vigor. BDB suggests it may denote fullness of oil or sap, aligning with the image of verdant, well-fed life.

senses.1: Applied to produce (Isa 30:23), righteous persons as thriving trees (Ps 92:14), and the prosperous or vigorous of the earth (Ps 22:29). The glosses emphasize richness, fullness of sap, and prosperity—conveying material and spiritual abundance. The word carries connotations of flourishing health and fruitfulness, not mere physical weight.

gloss_readable: A town in northern Israel, north of Samaria, where Joseph's brothers had moved their flocks (Gen 37:17) and where Elisha was surrounded by an Aramean army—until his servant's eyes were opened to see chariots of fire (2 Kgs 6:13). The site has been identified with modern Tell Dothan. All three occurrences appear in narrative settings involving travel or military movements, and the multilingual glosses uniformly preserve the proper name with minor orthographic variation (Dotan, Dotán).

senses.1: The proper noun consistently refers to a specific geographic location in the narratives of Joseph (Gen 37:17 twice) and Elisha (2 Kgs 6:13). Translations preserve the name rather than translate it, reflecting its function as a fixed toponym in biblical geography.

gloss_terse: remove, take away; drive out or send into exile
gloss_readable: This verb appears in wisdom and prophetic literature with the sense of removing or driving away. Proverbs uses it twice for removing dross from silver and the wicked from a king's presence (Prov 25:4–5), establishing a metaphor of purification. Isaiah 27:8 is debated—either God 'removed' (sent into exile) his people with a harsh wind, or he 'winnowed' them. The multilingual glosses (Spanish quita, arrojó; French enlever) support the core idea of forceful removal or expulsion.

senses.1: The verb denotes forceful removal in all three contexts: purging impurities (Prov 25:4), driving away the wicked (Prov 25:5), and sending into exile or sifting away (Isa 27:8). The cross-lingual evidence points to active expulsion or separation, whether physical, moral, or judicial.

gloss_terse: rumbling, growling, moaning; a sigh or sound of distress
gloss_readable: A noun evoking low, ominous sounds. It describes the 'rumbling' of thunder as God's voice (Job 37:2), the brevity of human life 'like a sigh' (Ps 90:9), and the content of Ezekiel's scroll: 'lamentations and mourning and woe' (Ezek 2:10). The multilingual glosses capture the affective register: Spanish suspiro y gemido, French murmure, German sigh. The word conveys both natural phenomena (thunder) and human expressions of grief or transience.

senses.1: The noun spans acoustic and emotional domains: the deep rumble of thunder (Job 37:2), the fleeting sound of a human sigh marking life's brevity (Ps 90:9), and the mournful utterances inscribed on a prophetic scroll (Ezek 2:10). The cross-lingual glosses highlight both the auditory quality (murmur, rumble) and the plaintive tone (sigh, mourning).

gloss_readable: A proper name with two referents: an Arabian tribe descended from Joktan (Gen 10:27; 1 Chr 1:21) and a son of the king of Hamath sent to David (1 Chr 18:10). The name appears in genealogical and diplomatic contexts, and is preserved across translations with minimal variation (Spanish Hadorán, French Hadoram). In 2 Samuel 8:10 the parallel text reads Joram, but the Greek and critical scholarship favor Hadoram as the original reading.

senses.1: Used for both a tribal eponym (Gen 10:27; 1 Chr 1:21) and an individual diplomat (1 Chr 18:10). Translators uniformly retain the proper name, recognizing its dual function in genealogy and historical narrative. The cross-linguistic uniformity reflects the conventional practice of not translating personal names.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic verb (Pael stem) appearing exclusively in Daniel, always with God as the object. Nebuchadnezzar 'honored' the Most High after his restoration (Dan 4:34, 37), and Daniel rebukes Belshazzar for failing to 'glorify' the God who holds his breath (Dan 5:23). The Spanish glorificaste and glorifiqué, along with French and German cognates, uniformly render the idea of giving honor and glory. This is cultic and royal language: acknowledging divine sovereignty.

senses.1: The verb appears three times in Daniel's Aramaic chapters, always directed toward God. Nebuchadnezzar glorifies God after humiliation and restoration (Dan 4:34, 37); Belshazzar is condemned for failing to do so (Dan 5:23). The multilingual glosses converge on the semantic field of honoring, glorifying, and exalting the divine.

gloss_terse: honor, majesty (especially of a king); Aramaic
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun denoting royal splendor and majesty, appearing in Daniel's account of Nebuchadnezzar's madness and restoration. The king's 'majesty' returned to him (Dan 4:30, 36), and God gave 'majesty' to Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 5:18). The Spanish mi majestad, French gloire, and the emphatic forms in Aramaic all point to outward dignity and sovereign grandeur. The word evokes the visible trappings of kingship and divine favor.

senses.1: The noun describes the royal dignity and visible splendor that Nebuchadnezzar lost and regained (Dan 4:30, 36) and which God had granted him (Dan 5:18). Cross-lingual glosses (majesty, gloire) consistently reflect the high-status, honorific sense. This is not inner virtue but the external manifestation of sovereign authority.

gloss_readable: A proper name borne by several individuals in postexilic lists (1 Chr 5:24; 9:7; Ezra 2:40). The etymology is debated: BDB mentions a possible abstract noun meaning 'songs of praise' or an infinitive 'praising,' though the personal-name function predominates. Translations preserve the name with slight orthographic variation (Spanish Hodavías, y-Hodavya). The name appears in genealogical and census contexts, identifying heads of families or Levitical groups.

senses.1: Used as a personal name in three genealogical or census lists (1 Chr 5:24; 9:7; Ezra 2:40). The multilingual glosses treat it as a proper noun, preserving transliteration rather than attempting semantic translation. Any etymological connection to praise remains background information, not activated in these contexts.

gloss_readable: A noun of doom and destruction. Isaiah warns that 'disaster shall fall upon you' (Isa 47:11), and Ezekiel prophesies 'disaster upon disaster' coming (Ezek 7:26, repeated twice in the verse for rhetorical effect). The Spanish calamidad and French malheur capture the catastrophic, overwhelming force of the word. This is not ordinary trouble but cascading ruin—divine judgment unfolding in waves.

senses.1: The noun denotes calamity and disaster in prophetic judgment oracles. It describes ruin falling on Babylon (Isa 47:11) and successive waves of disaster on Jerusalem (Ezek 7:26). The multilingual evidence (calamity, malheur) uniformly points to sudden, overwhelming catastrophe. The repetition in Ezekiel ('disaster upon disaster') emphasizes relentless, cumulative devastation.

gloss_readable: A theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh has saved.' It identifies a prince of Judah in Nehemiah's dedication ceremony (Neh 12:32) and the father of Jezaniah, a military leader in Jeremiah's time (Jer 42:1; 43:2). The name reflects the theology of deliverance embedded in Hebrew onomastics. Translations preserve the name (Spanish Hosaías, Osaías), honoring its function as a personal identifier rather than translating its etymological meaning.

senses.1: Appears as a personal name in both narrative (Jer 42:1; 43:2) and liturgical (Neh 12:32) contexts. The cross-lingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name. Its theological meaning ('Yah has saved') remains implicit, activating the broader pattern of salvific hope in Israelite naming practices.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic verb describing movement and conduct. It appears in Daniel's vision of the fiery furnace, where four men 'walk' unharmed in the flames (Dan 3:25), and in the account of Nebuchadnezzar 'walking' on his palace roof (Dan 4:29) and later 'walking in pride' (Dan 4:37). The Spanish andan, paseando ('strolling, walking about') and the French/German glosses all emphasize literal or metaphorical movement. The verb can denote physical locomotion or ethical conduct ('walk in pride').

senses.1: The verb appears in literal (Dan 3:25, 4:29) and metaphorical (Dan 4:37) walking contexts. The men in the furnace 'walk about' miraculously unharmed; Nebuchadnezzar 'walks' on his roof and later 'walks in pride.' Cross-lingual glosses capture both physical movement (walking, paseando) and ethical comportment (walk in pride).

gloss_readable: An Aramaic fiscal term denoting taxes or tolls imposed by imperial authority. It appears in Ezra's correspondence about Persian revenue concerns: opponents warn that Jerusalem will not pay 'toll, custom, or tribute' (Ezra 4:13, 20), and Artaxerxes exempts temple personnel from such levies (Ezra 7:24). The Spanish y-peaje, French contribution, and German Toll-related glosses all reflect taxation vocabulary. This is administrative language from the Achaemenid bureaucracy.

senses.1: A fiscal term for tolls or taxes in three Ezra passages (Ezra 4:13, 20; 7:24). The context is Persian imperial revenue and exemptions for temple workers. Multilingual glosses converge on taxation semantics (toll, peaje, contribution), reflecting the administrative register of Aramaic correspondence under Persian rule.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic conjunction marking logical inference or tentative condition. In Daniel, it introduces royal commands ('therefore tell me the dream,' Dan 2:6, 9) and advice ('therefore, O king, accept my counsel,' Dan 4:27). BDB notes a debate whether it always means 'therefore' or sometimes 'only/perhaps.' The Spanish por tanto, tal vez and French si, German deshalb reflect both inferential and conditional nuances. The word signals rhetorical transition and reasoning.

senses.1: Functions as a logical connector in Aramaic discourse: 'therefore' in Dan 2:6, 9 (introducing a demand) and Dan 4:27 (introducing advice). The multilingual evidence shows both inferential (therefore, por tanto) and conditional (perhaps, si) senses. The word marks transitions in argument and royal rhetoric.

gloss_readable: A city name in Assyrian boasts of conquest, listed alongside Sepharvaim and Ivvah (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). The Assyrian king taunts: 'Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?' The site is unknown, though scholars suggest a location in Syria or Mesopotamia. Translations preserve the name (Spanish Hena, Hená) without attempting to identify or translate it.

senses.1: A toponym appearing in Assyrian conquest rhetoric (2 Kgs 18:34; 19:13; Isa 37:13). The multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name, reflecting its function as a fixed geographic referent in political propaganda. Its location remains unknown, but the rhetorical function is clear: invoking fallen cities to intimidate Jerusalem.

gloss_readable: A noun denoting the state or moment of conceiving offspring. God tells Eve 'I will greatly multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children' (Gen 3:16, where 'conception' is parallel to 'childbearing'). The LORD 'gave her conception' and Ruth bore a son (Ruth 4:13). Hosea laments Israel's loss of blessing 'from birth, from the womb, from conception' (Hos 9:11). The Spanish concepción, tu concepción and French grossesse, conception reflect both the initial act and the state of pregnancy.

senses.1: Refers to the act or state of conceiving a child in three contexts: the curse after Eden (Gen 3:16), Ruth's miraculous conception (Ruth 4:13), and the loss of blessing in Hosea (Hos 9:11). Cross-lingual glosses (conception, concepción, grossesse) emphasize both the moment of conception and the resulting pregnancy, often in parallel with birth imagery.

gloss_terse: Zebulonite, of the tribe of Zebulun (gentilic)
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective identifying members of the tribe of Zebulun. It appears as 'the Zebulonite' for the judge Elon (Judg 12:11, 12) and collectively for the census count of 'the Zebulunites' (Num 26:27). The Spanish zabulonita(s) and French/German cognates all reflect the tribal-affiliation function. This is standard gentilic morphology: a proper noun transformed into an adjective or collective noun identifying descendants or members.

senses.1: Functions as a tribal gentilic in census (Num 26:27) and narrative (Judg 12:11, 12) contexts. The multilingual glosses uniformly render the tribal affiliation (Zebulonite, zabulonita, Zebulunite). The word identifies individuals or groups by descent from Zebulun, Jacob's tenth son.

gloss_terse: tremble, quake (in fear or physical shaking)
gloss_readable: A verb of trembling, whether from fear, awe, or physical shaking. Haman 'trembled' before Esther (Esth 5:9), the 'keepers of the house' (hands or arms) 'tremble' in old age (Eccl 12:3), and Habakkuk envisions creditors who will 'shake' Babylon violently (Hab 2:7). The Spanish tembló, que tiemblen and German/French cognates capture both the involuntary physical response and the violent shaking inflicted by others. The word can be passive (trembling with fear) or causative (shaking violently).

senses.1: Describes trembling from fear (Esth 5:9), the shaking of limbs in old age (Eccl 12:3), and the violent shaking of judgment (Hab 2:7). The multilingual glosses reflect both involuntary tremor (trembled, tiemblen) and forceful agitation (shake, sacuden). The semantic range spans emotional, physiological, and violent domains.

gloss_terse: press, squeeze, wring out (liquid from something)
gloss_readable: A verb denoting pressure applied to extract liquid or crush underfoot. Gideon 'squeezed' a fleece and wrung out dew (Judg 6:38), ostrich eggs may be 'crushed' underfoot (Job 39:15), and a viper's egg when 'pressed' (or hatched?) releases danger (Isa 59:5). The sore in Isaiah 1:6 has 'not been pressed out'—not drained or treated. The Spanish exprimió, los aplastará and French/German squeeze/crush glosses all emphasize forceful compression or extraction.

senses.1: The verb appears in contexts of squeezing out liquid (Judg 6:38), crushing underfoot (Job 39:15), and failing to press/treat a wound (Isa 1:6, passive). The multilingual evidence (squeezed, exprimió, crush, aplastará) points to applying pressure to extract, compress, or destroy. The semantic core is forceful manipulation of solid or semi-solid matter.

gloss_readable: A gentilic noun for the people of Ziph, a town in the hill country of Judah. The Ziphites twice betrayed David to Saul, reporting his hiding place (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1). Psalm 54's superscription recalls this treachery: 'when the Ziphites came and told Saul,
' The Spanish zifeos and French/German cognates uniformly render the tribal or local affiliation. This is a case where geography becomes moral identity: the Ziphites are remembered as informants.

senses.1: Identifies the inhabitants of Ziph in narratives of their betrayal of David (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1; Ps 54:1). The multilingual glosses (Ziphites, zifeos, Ziphien) consistently reflect the gentilic function. The term evokes not just geography but the moral character of those who informed against David.

gloss_terse: missile, spark, firebrand; flying or leaping projectile
gloss_readable: A noun denoting projectiles or sparks—things that leap or fly. It describes 'firebrands and arrows' shot in deadly jest (Prov 26:18), 'kindlers of fire' who 'gird themselves with firebrands' (Isa 50:11, twice). The root suggests something that shoots forth or springs up: either fire-missiles, sparks, or brands. The Spanish chispas and the French/German glosses (זקים, זיקות) reflect the image of leaping, flying fire. This is weaponized or dangerous fire—unpredictable and destructive.

senses.1: Refers to fiery projectiles or sparks in three contexts: deadly missiles (Prov 26:18), and firebrands kindled in judgment (Isa 50:11, twice). The multilingual glosses (firebrands, chispas, זקים) emphasize the flying, leaping quality of fire. The word evokes danger, unpredictability, and the violence of flame.

gloss_terse: Zaccai (personal name; possibly abbreviated from Zechariah)
gloss_readable: A personal name appearing in postexilic lists of returnees: a family head in Ezra 2:9 and Nehemiah 7:14, and possibly the same individual in Nehemiah 3:20 (though the Greek suggests variant traditions). BDB notes a proposal that Zaccai is an abbreviated form of Zechariah. Translations preserve the name with slight variation (Spanish Zacai, Zaccai). The name appears in genealogical and census contexts, identifying a family lineage among the exiles who returned to Judah.

senses.1: A proper name in three postexilic genealogical or census lists (Ezra 2:9; Neh 3:20; 7:14). The multilingual glosses transliterate the name, reflecting its function as a personal identifier. Any etymological connection to Zechariah remains speculative background, not semantically active in these texts.

gloss_terse: raging heat, scorching wind; burning indignation
gloss_readable: A noun evoking intense, destructive heat—whether physical or emotional. It describes the 'scorching heat of famine' that darkens skin (Lam 5:10), the 'burning wind' sent as divine judgment alongside fire and brimstone (Ps 11:6), and the 'burning indignation' that seizes the psalmist over the wicked (Ps 119:53). The Spanish ardor, abrasador and French horreur capture the consuming, oppressive force. This is heat that wounds—fever, sirocco, or fury.

senses.1: Denotes destructive heat in three forms: feverish heat from famine (Lam 5:10), scorching judgment wind (Ps 11:6), and emotional burning indignation (Ps 119:53). The multilingual evidence (scorching heat, ardor, horreur) reflects both physical and affective registers. The semantic core is overwhelming, consuming intensity—whether meteorological, somatic, or moral.

gloss_readable: A Levitical name (Gershonite clan) appearing in genealogical lists in Chronicles (1 Chr 6:20, 42; 2 Chr 29:12). The name is etymologically related to the word for 'lewdness' or 'wickedness,' though in these contexts it functions purely as a personal identifier without moral connotation. Translations preserve the name (Spanish Zima, French/German Zimmah). The name highlights the complexity of Hebrew onomastics: not all names activate their etymological meanings.

senses.1: A personal name identifying Levites in three genealogical contexts (1 Chr 6:20, 42; 2 Chr 29:12). The cross-lingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name, treating it as a fixed identifier. Although the root suggests 'lewdness,' the name here carries no pejorative force—illustrating the gap between etymology and usage.

gloss_readable: A late Hebrew (Aramaic-influenced) verb appearing only as a Pual participle, describing times that are 'fixed' or 'appointed.' It appears in Ezra and Nehemiah's cultic and administrative reforms: 'at appointed times' for legal hearings (Ezra 10:14), for wood offerings (Neh 10:34), and for offerings at fixed festivals (Neh 13:31). The Spanish señalados and French/German cognates all reflect the idea of predetermined, scheduled times. This is liturgical and bureaucratic language: the ordering of time by decree.

senses.1: Describes 'appointed times' in three postexilic administrative or cultic contexts (Ezra 10:14; Neh 10:34; 13:31). The multilingual glosses (appointed, señalados) uniformly reflect temporal fixity and scheduling. The word denotes times set by authority—whether for legal assemblies or ritual observances.

gloss_readable: A verb specific to viticultural practice: pruning grapevines. It appears in the Sabbath-year legislation ('you shall prune your vineyard,' Lev 25:3) and its suspension during the Sabbath year ('you shall not prune,' Lev 25:4). Isaiah prophesies a vineyard that 'will not be pruned or hoed' (Isa 5:6), signaling abandonment. The Spanish podarás, French tu devra prune, and German du soll prune all preserve the agricultural specificity. This is skilled labor: the careful cutting that promotes fruitfulness.

senses.1: Refers to the agricultural practice of pruning vines in three contexts: command (Lev 25:3), prohibition (Lev 25:4), and abandonment (Isa 5:6, passive). The multilingual glosses uniformly render the viticultural action (prune, podarás). The word evokes the rhythm of agricultural care and its cessation—whether by law (Sabbath) or judgment (Isaiah's vineyard).

gloss_terse: melody, song (especially in praise of Yahweh)
gloss_readable: A noun denoting musical praise, whether instrumental or vocal. It appears in liturgical summons ('Take up a psalm; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp,' Ps 81:2), in the threefold confession 'The LORD is my strength and my song' (Exod 15:2; Ps 118:14; Isa 12:2), and in the sound of harp and melody (Ps 98:5). The Spanish mi canción, y-mi-cántico and French chant reflect the devotional, celebratory register. This is music offered to God—joyful, public, and often accompanied by instruments.

senses.1: Denotes musical praise in three thematic clusters: the LORD as 'my song' (Exod 15:2; Ps 118:14; Isa 12:2) and instrumental or vocal music in worship (Ps 81:2; 98:5; cf. Amos 5:23). The multilingual glosses (song, mi canción, chant) emphasize the celebratory and cultic function. The word evokes communal, joyous worship—not private lament.

gloss_readable: A late Hebrew noun denoting categories or types. It appears in Psalm 144:13 ('our garners full, providing all kinds of produce,' lit. 'from kind to kind') and in the account of Asa's burial with 'various kinds of spices' (2 Chr 16:14). The Spanish de especie a especie, y-variedades and French/German kind, von kind emphasize taxonomic diversity. This is the language of abundance and variety: not one type but all types, a fullness that spans categories.

senses.1: Refers to varieties or kinds in two contexts: agricultural produce (Ps 144:13, 'from kind to kind' = all sorts) and spices (2 Chr 16:14). The multilingual glosses (kind, especie, variedades) uniformly reflect categorical diversity. The word conveys plenitude through enumeration of types—a fullness that transcends singular categories.

gloss_readable: A noun denoting pitch or tar, a waterproofing agent. Moses' mother 'daubed' his basket 'with bitumen and pitch' (Exod 2:3), and Isaiah prophesies that Edom's 'streams shall be turned to pitch' and 'her land shall become burning pitch' (Isa 34:9, twice). The Spanish brea and French poix reflect the sticky, flammable substance used both for preservation (Moses' ark) and as a symbol of judgment (Edom's desolation). Pitch evokes both protection and destruction—sealing life or sealing doom.

senses.1: Refers to bituminous pitch in three contexts: waterproofing Moses' basket (Exod 2:3) and prophetic imagery of Edom's streams and land turned to burning pitch (Isa 34:9, twice). The multilingual glosses (pitch, brea, poix) uniformly denote the tar-like substance. The word carries dual valence: protective sealant and apocalyptic fire fuel.

gloss_readable: A river in Upper Mesopotamia, flowing into the Euphrates from the east. It is called 'the river Gozan' (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11) and appears in the account of the Assyrian deportation of Israelites. First Chronicles 5:26 lists 'Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan' (the first two may be scribal variants of the same name). The name is preserved across translations (Spanish Habor, Jabor; French Chavor). This is a geographic marker of exile: the place where Israel was scattered.

senses.1: A river name in three deportation contexts (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:11; 1 Chr 5:26). The multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the toponym (Habor, Jabor, Chavor). The river functions as a geographic referent for the Assyrian exile—a fixed point on the map of Israel's dispersion.

gloss_terse: be in labor, travail; give birth with pain (Piel)
gloss_readable: A verb of childbirth pain and labor. The wicked man 'conceives trouble and gives birth to deceit' (Ps 7:14, metaphorical travail). In the Song, the beloved's mother 'was in labor with you' and 'brought you forth in pain' (Song 8:5, twice). The Spanish tuvo dolores de parto, concibe and French a enfanté dans la douleur reflect the physical and metaphorical anguish of bringing forth. The word evokes the labor of creation—whether of life or of evil schemes.

senses.1: Describes labor pains in literal (Song 8:5, twice) and metaphorical (Ps 7:14) contexts. The wicked 'conceive' and 'travail' with evil; the mother travails to bring forth a child. Cross-lingual glosses (in labor, dolores de parto, enfanté dans la douleur) uniformly reflect the painful, strenuous process of bringing forth—whether child or wickedness.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun denoting harm or damage. It appears when opponents warn that a rebuilt Jerusalem will cause 'damage' to royal revenue (Ezra 4:22), and in Daniel's accounts of protection from harm: the men in the fiery furnace have 'no hurt' (Dan 3:25) and Daniel emerges from the lions' den 'without injury' (Dan 6:23). The Spanish daño, herida and French dommage reflect both physical and financial harm. This is administrative and narrative language: the absence or threat of damage.

senses.1: Denotes harm or damage in three contexts: fiscal damage to the king (Ezra 4:22), absence of physical harm in the furnace (Dan 3:25), and deliverance from injury in the lions' den (Dan 6:23). The multilingual glosses (damage, hurt, daño, dommage) span financial and somatic domains. The word evokes threat and deliverance: what could harm but does not, or what will harm if unchecked.

gloss_readable: A noun denoting a pledge taken as security for a loan. It appears in Ezekiel's descriptions of righteous and wicked conduct: the righteous 'restores the pledge' (Ezek 18:16; 33:15), while the wicked keeps it (Ezek 18:12). The word derives from the verb 'to bind' and reflects the legal-economic practice of holding collateral. The Spanish prenda and French/German cognates all denote the object held as surety. This is covenant and commerce language: what binds debtor to creditor, and what justice demands be returned.

senses.1: Refers to the pledge or collateral taken as security in three Ezekiel contexts (Ezek 18:12, 16; 33:15). The righteous restore it; the wicked do not. Multilingual glosses (pledge, prenda) uniformly reflect the legal-economic practice of holding security. The word evokes the ethical demands of lending: not exploiting the vulnerable by keeping what must be returned.

gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun for comrade or associate. It appears in Daniel's account of the dream crisis: the decree to kill 'Daniel and his companions' (Dan 2:13), and Daniel's plea for 'mercy concerning this mystery for Daniel and his companions' (Dan 2:17, 18). The Spanish sus compañeros and French/German cognates all denote social and professional peers. This is the language of solidarity: those who share Daniel's fate and faith, standing together before the king's decree.

senses.1: Refers to Daniel's companions (Hananiah, Mishael, Azariah) in three contexts of crisis and prayer (Dan 2:13, 17, 18). The multilingual glosses (companions, compañeros, חברוהי) uniformly reflect association and fellowship. The word evokes shared risk and mutual support: those bound together by circumstance and covenant.

gloss_terse: clefts, crevices (of rock); places of concealment
gloss_readable: A noun denoting narrow fissures or clefts in rock, serving as hiding places. The beloved is called 'my dove in the clefts of the rock' (Song 2:14), a tender image of intimacy and refuge. But the same imagery turns ominous in prophetic judgment: Edom 'dwelling in the clefts of the rock' (Jer 49:16; Obad 3) trusts in inaccessible strongholds—yet will be brought down. The Spanish hendiduras and French fentes emphasize the narrow, hidden character. Clefts offer safety—or the illusion of it.

senses.1: Refers to rock clefts as places of refuge or concealment in three contexts: the beloved hidden in safety (Song 2:14) and Edom's arrogant trust in mountain strongholds (Jer 49:16; Obad 3). The multilingual glosses (clefts, hendiduras, fentes) uniformly denote narrow fissures. The word evokes both protective refuge and false security—depending on who seeks shelter.

gloss_readable: A personal name and gentilic: Haggi, son of Gad (Gen 46:16), the eponymous ancestor of the Haggite clan (Num 26:15, twice). The name means 'festal' and appears in census and genealogical lists. Translations preserve the name (Spanish Hagui, Jagi; French Haggi). This is standard onomastic and gentilic usage: a personal name becomes the marker of tribal identity, tracing descent from Jacob through Gad to Haggi's family.

senses.1: Functions as a personal name (Gen 46:16) and gentilic (Num 26:15, twice). The multilingual glosses (Haggi, Hagui, Haggite) reflect both the individual and the clan. The name evokes the broader pattern of Israelite genealogy: from patriarch to tribe to clan, each name a thread in the covenant lineage.

gloss_readable: A verb of joy and gladness. Jethro 'rejoiced' over all the good the LORD had done for Israel (Exod 18:9), Job curses the day of his birth that it should 'not rejoice among the days of the year' (Job 3:6), and the psalmist declares that God 'makes him glad with joy' (Ps 21:6). The Spanish se alegró, le alegras and French se réjouir capture the affective warmth. This is not mere happiness but a response to goodness—whether God's deliverance or the gift of life itself (or its tragic absence).

senses.1: Describes rejoicing in three contexts: Jethro's joy over Israel's deliverance (Exod 18:9), the banishment of joy from Job's birth-day (Job 3:6), and God making the king glad (Ps 21:6). The multilingual glosses (rejoiced, se alegró, se réjouir) uniformly reflect exuberant gladness. The word evokes response to blessing or its absence—joy as recognition of divine favor.

gloss_readable: A town in Benjamin, listed with Lod and Ono in postexilic census lists (Ezra 2:33; Neh 7:37; 11:34). It is identified with modern El-Haditheh, a few miles northeast of Lydda. The name appears in administrative contexts: counting returnees and resettled towns. Translations preserve the name (Spanish Hadid, Jadid). This is the geography of restoration: small towns repopulated after exile, their names a litany of hope and return.

senses.1: A place name in three postexilic lists (Ezra 2:33; Neh 7:37; 11:34), always grouped with Lod and Ono. The multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name (Hadid, Jadid). The town functions as a marker of the province of Benjamin's resettlement—a fixed point on the map of restored Judah.

gloss_readable: An adjective of absence or cessation. The psalmist asks 'let me know how fleeting I am' (Ps 39:4, or 'how transient'). Isaiah describes the Servant as 'despised and rejected by men' (Isa 53:3, lit. 'lacking men' or 'forsaken by men'). Ezekiel distinguishes the one who 'hears' from 'the one who refuses' (Ezek 3:27). The Spanish frágil, rechazado and French abandonner, cesser reflect both temporal and relational dimensions: what is fleeting or what is forsaken. The word evokes lack—whether of time, support, or obedience.

senses.1: Describes that which ceases, is transient, or is forsaken in three contexts: human life's brevity (Ps 39:4), the Servant forsaken by people (Isa 53:3), and the one who refuses to listen (Ezek 3:27). The multilingual glosses (transient, frágil, abandonner, cesser) reflect both temporal ephemerality and social abandonment. The word evokes vulnerability and absence.

gloss_terse: circle, vault, horizon (of earth or heavens)
gloss_readable: A noun denoting the circular vault or horizon of the cosmos. God 'sits above the circle of the earth' (Isa 40:22), 'inscribed a circle on the face of the deep' at creation (Prov 8:27), and 'walks on the vault of heaven' (Job 22:14). The Spanish círculo and French/German circle/vault glosses evoke both the two-dimensional horizon and the three-dimensional dome. This is cosmological language: the geometry of creation, where God's throne transcends the bounded sphere of the world.

senses.1: Refers to the circular boundary or vault of the cosmos in three poetic contexts: God enthroned above the earth's circle (Isa 40:22), the circle inscribed at creation (Prov 8:27), and God's circuit of the heavens (Job 22:14). The multilingual glosses (circle, círculo, vault) reflect ancient cosmology's image of a bounded, vaulted world. The word evokes divine transcendence over created order.
